documents.subject: Washington/Baltimore Newspaper Guild Local 35 bulletin on newsroom pay gaps by race and sex, responding to the Task Force on the Newsroom (Mike Geller report)

pages.transcript:
POST GUILD BULLETIN
[handwritten: 30]
Washington/Baltimore Newspaper Guild
Local 35  No. 23  Date Nov. 23, 1993
Your Guild supports you. Support your Guild!

Creating A Fair, Diverse Newsroom: The Missing Chapter

You may have seen the report by the Task Force on the Newsroom, which was headed by Mike Geller, assistant managing editor for foreign news. The report is a serious look at a problem that those of us in the newsroom have recognized for years: that our workplace has been moving too slowly to become a diverse workplace in which members of ethnic minority groups, women and gays feel equally welcomed, valued and challenged. The Task Force makes substantial recommendations that, if implemented, could go a long way toward creating a more diverse, civilized and productive workplace. The Guild leadership thinks that, if you care about these issues, you have a responsibility to take the couple of hours necessary to digest the report. We think there should be wide-ranging discussion of the report and its implications.

The Post Still Pays Black and Women Employees Less

The Post's difficulty in keeping and developing good reporters of all ethnic backgrounds and both genders has an important root that was not within the scope of the Task Force. The Post continues to pay women and minorities much less, across the board, than it does white men.

In 1991, the last year for which the Guild has salary data, our black reporters earned, on average, $6,299 less than our white reporters. Women earned $10,355 less than men. Our 1990 data, which have been further broken down, show similar gaps even when the reporters being compared have the same length of service with the Post. While two individual reporters' salaries might legitimately differ because of their relative performance, that could not be the case between racial groups or the sexes.

For years, the Guild has researched and publicized these gaps and others -- involving Hispanics, older employees and commercial departments as well as the newsroom. Since 1988, the Guild has had a complaint -- alleging pay discrimination based on sex, race and age -- at the D.C. Office of Human Rights.

Now, since newsroom management seems intent on dealing with the issues raised by the Task Force, we all may have an opportunity to reconsider the salary gaps, which effectively form a "missing chapter" in the discussion of why The Washington Post newsroom is not seen as a workplace that treats us all equally. The Guild will, in coming days, publish a more detailed report on the salary gaps to promote that discussion.

The Road Behind . . . And Ahead

Both the Guild and newsroom management have wrestled with the broad issue here for years -- with too little to show for it. The goals of the 1986 Hoagland commission on the newsroom are unfulfilled, as are those of the Guild's pay discrimination complaint. In the past few years, two rounds of settlement talks on the Guild's complaint have failed. But we think that two groups of people working toward the same goal -- a diverse and humane workplace -- ought to be able to do so together.

-- Jim Rupert
Unit Chair

documents.title: Declaration/Affidavit of Martha M. Hamilton, page 9 (paragraphs 29-32)
documents.subject: Martha Hamilton's own numbered narrative statement describing her reporting assignments (1995-1997 peso crisis, enterprise stories, fellowships, energy/utility beat) and comparisons to colleagues' pay and merit increases
documents.date: unknown (content covers 1994-1997; part of the ~1997-98 settlement arbitration filings)
documents.notes: Typed page numbered '- 9 -' at bottom; paragraphs 29-32 of a first-person sworn-style statement by the claimant ('I'), identified in the collection as Martha M. Hamilton. Final sentence is cut off mid-page ('...global climate change'). First line starts paragraph 29, so this is a continuation page.

pages.transcript:
29. In 1995, I helped cover the crash of the Mexican peso and the fallout from the peso crisis in 1996, including traveling to Mexico to write about the impact on investment. Despite divorce proceeding which often required me to be away from work and taking into account a five week absence on fellowship, I still wrote five front page stories and five stories for the Sunday business front in 1995. During the same year, Warren Brown, who had the high profile auto industry beat, had six front page stories. He received a merit pay increase, and I didn't.

30. During the Ignatius years, I also contributed many enterprise pieces that ended up on the front page, including an economic history of air conditioning and the recycling of soda bottles into polar fleece(1994), the use of NASCAR racing as a marketing vehicle (1996), stories about global warming (1998). These were stories that I conceptualized and produced, not stories that got on the front page because they were major breaking news.

31. During this period I also was one of 12 reporters nationwide who won a fellowship to a National Press Foundation seminar on environmental issues (1994). In addition, in October 1995, I was one of about a dozen U.S. fellows selected by the Eisenhower Foundation Fellowship to study abroad. I was the first woman fellow ever selected to be sent to Taiwan.)

32. In 1997, because Dan Southerland, who had been covering energy, had left and it appeared that utility deregulation was a major, breaking story, I began covering oil, energy and utilities and the intersection of business and the environment in addition to national general assignments. I suggested to David Ignatius that I do so, and he concurred. I must assume that Southerland's salary was much higher than mine. My work during this period included extensive coverage of electric utility deregulation and mergers and acquisitions. I was frequent commentator on radio, television and live discussions of the issues. Oil industry coverage included consumer issues, the industry's reaction to the global climate change issues, OPEC and the challenges facing the industry in a global economy. Environmental coverage included stories on alternative energy, the economic impact of El Nino and participation in the Post's global climate change

- 9 -

documents.subject: Narrative by Paul Bluestein comparing colleague Peter Behr's salary history, starting salary, merit increases, and experience/education to Martha Hamilton's, per the 1993-2002 salary snapshots
documents.date: unknown (references 'As of September 1, 2002'; prepared under agreed arbitration procedures for settlement purposes)

pages.transcript:
CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION UNDER THE AGREED ARBITRATION PROCEDURES
PREPARED FOR SETTLEMENT PURPOSES

Peter Behr was paid substantially more than Hamilton on the 1993 to 2002 salary snapshots.

Experience and Education
Behr came to The Post in the early 1980s as a reporter in Financial News. He became an editor in Financial News in 1982, returning to his reporter position in 1983. He became the Editor of National Weekly in 1987 and later that year he became the Assistant Managing Editor for Business and Financial. In 1993 he returned to a reporter position where he remains today. Prior to starting at The Post, Behr worked at the Baltimore Sun as a News Editor and reporter for approximately three years. He also spent some six years as a reporter for the Times Union and eight years as a reporter for the Gannett News Service. Behr is a graduate of Harvard University. He also received a Nieman Fellowship from Harvard.

Starting Salary
Upon starting at The Post, Behr received approximately a three percent increase over his prior salary at the Baltimore Sun. His starting salary was slightly more than the salary of Hamilton at that time.

Salary History
Behr received salary increases when he became an editor in Financial News, the Editor of National Weekly and the Assistant Managing Editor for Business and Financial. As of September 1, 2002, he had received eight merit increases during his time at The Post - one of which was given during his time as an editor in Financial News. The seven merit increases he received as a reporter in Financial News were received in the following years: 1981, 1983, 1984, 1985 and 1986.

Explanation:
Behr received substantial raises when he became an editor in Financial News, the Editor of National Weekly and the Assistant Managing Editor in Financial News. He retained his editor's salary when he returned to work as a reporter in Financial News.

Behr was paid a high salary by his previous employer - slightly more than the salary of Hamilton at The Post at that time. Therefore, when Behr began at The Post, his starting salary was also slightly more than the salary of Hamilton at that time.

Paul Bluestein

documents.title: Task Force Newsroom Survey — Employee Verbatim Responses, page 3
documents.subject: Compiled anonymous survey responses from Post employees (labeled by race, sex, age, and desk) on race relations, treatment of blacks and women, promotions, and diversity in the newsroom
documents.date: unknown (contemporary with the 1993 Task Force on the Newsroom era)
documents.notes: Two-column typed page with quoted survey answers under bold descriptive headers (e.g. 'White female, Metro, Reporter:'), page numbered '3' at bottom center. Top edge of the sheet is folded/cropped so the first header line on the left column is partly cut off (visible as 'e male, National/Financial/Investigative/Foreign, Reporter:' — almost certainly 'White male, ...'). Content clearly continues from a prior page. Classified as `other` (survey compilation); likely assembled as arbitration background material.

pages.transcript:
[left column, header partly cut off at top: '...e male, National/Financial/Investigative/Foreign, Reporter:']
What does "enough" blacks mean? What is The Post seeking to achieve if it sets a 30-percent minority quota? Newsroom mix? Change in coverage?

I think it is silly and arbitrary to hire on the basis of color or gender: if The Post improves the quality of newsroom conditions top minority and women candidates will come here. Frankly, if you want good black reporters, support the ASNE minority-internship reporters and "feeder" programs with other newspapers.

White female, National/Financial/Investigative/Foreign, Reporter:

I think this young survey reflects racism — The problem at The Post is that young, hard-working, talented blacks, whites, men and women have no place to move up...There are few if any openings on national or foreign — and often they fill those by hiring from outside...so EVERYBODY feels frustrated...There is little "career development" here, (i.e. opportunity for growth)...Blacks may leave simply because they have better options (i.e. other news media looking to hire more blacks)...I would love to stay and grow at The Post if I felt there was a good chance to move up, but I feel like I'm going to do what I'm doing now indefinitely — and if some other news organization offered me a chance to go overseas or be a national reporter I would do it...

The reason I say this is racist is that the white editors and some blacks only perceive black frustrations here. What about the rest of us?

White female, National/Financial/Investigative/Foreign, Editor:

I think that cronyism has more to do with promotions and assignments than any other factor, although one certainly could find exceptions to that rule, like any other rule. Yes, I'm a white woman, and yes, I've seen other women — and men — get hired and paid because they're black. I think The Post is a better place than most for blacks, but that doesn't make us great. We get all excited, go on a recruitment campaign — then not hire the best people. We've done that in many cases — blacks, women, reporting specialties — you name it. Our vices are not necessarily racist at their inception, but they certainly work out that way. We're so careful hiring some people, and not really careful enough with others. In my experience here, I'm the wrong sex, the wrong age, the wrong color — pick your excuse — whenever that reason is convenient. The fact that I'm good doesn't count.

White female, Style/News Desk/Sports/Editorial/Other, Editor:

I feel women clearly are not represented in top management at The Post. I am treated well, but never expect a shot at the top, in part because of what appears a pattern of no women at the top (except in Style, formerly the "women's section"). I'm not black but if I were, I'd feel I had two strikes against me. And I don't feel it's fair to concentrate on promoting blacks, or add essentially an AME/blacks, and insult women. This smacks of tokenism, although surely not so intedend, I'm sure.

White female, National/Financial/Investigative/Foreign, Reporter:

A lot of the above represents impressions rather than certain knowledge. I don't think Post management is very candid about salaries or about their opinions of staffers' work and value — black or white.

[right column]
White female, Metro, Reporter:

Your survey should cover The Post's disinterest in keeping most of the employees it already has, black or white. Management is childlike in wanting to be dazzled and distracted by new faces rather than cultivating the expensive and top-notch personnel it already has on board. This fickle desire for the newest, the latest, etc. is the reason the product is so erratic and explains why The Post will never be the comprehensive, authoritative and vital force that the New York Times is. It's a problem that can be corrected, but it means that editors will have to develop independence of mind, rather than constantly guessing which way the winds of the top offices are blowing.

Black male, Reporter:

That there are no black editors at the level of AME involved in the news management of The Washington Post is, in itself, a glaring sign of an absence of equal opportunity in the newsroom. I am not counting Matthew Lewis as a news editor. Matt's elevation to AME leaves one with the impression that in order to move up the management ladder, you have to win a Pulitzer if you are a black male.

White male, 30 or under, Style/News Desk/Sports/Editorial/Other, Reporter:

The Post has been wonderful to me, they gave me a chance when no one else would. I will be eternally grateful. The color is of no importance, if you are willing to work, they will see that you get ahead. I have always been treated fairly and I appreciate the fact that "management" cares enough to even look into the feelings of minority employes. It is really a great and fair place to work.

White female, Metro, Reporter:

I think the biggest problem at The Post affecting personnel, which affects mainly women and blacks, is the arbitrary and un-sought out assessment of a person's work. Most assessments are characteristics as thoroughness, attitude toward work, accuracy and general ability. They prefer to judge a person by how will they do in politic[ing] in the office.

White male, over 30, National/Financial/Investigative/Foreign, Reporter

No questions about gays. It's a legitimate question. Had there been, response would be more negative. More depends on educational background and general demeanor than race or sex. Nobody asked about Jews. Gays should have been included between blacks and whites. The comparison between other newspapers. i.e., New York Times: senior editor positions held by Jews, not so at Post.

White male, six years or more, older than 30, National/Financial/Investigative/Foreign, Reporter:

The Post is losing its guts. Let's get our guts back.

3

pages.transcript:
[handwritten at top right: 31]

CLAIM FORM

Under a settlement agreement between the Washington-Baltimore Newspaper Guild and the Washington Post, a procedure for final and binding arbitration has been created to hear certain claims of alleged discrimination in wages or other compensation.

To be eligible to file a claim:

-  You must be a current employee of The Washington Post.

-  You must currently, or you must have at some period between September 1, 1994 and the present, been employed in a Guild-covered position at the Post.

-  You must sign a statement that you believe in good faith that you were discriminated against on the basis of your gender, race and/or Hispanic origin in connection with your wages or other compensation in a Guild-covered position at the Post at some time between September 1, 1994 and the present. If the alleged discrimination is claimed to have begun before September 1, 1994, a claim may be asserted as long as the discrimination continued after that date.

-  You must abide by the procedures applicable to the arbitration process. Those procedures are attached to this Claim Form.

-  The Claim Form must be delivered, or postmarked for delivery, to Carol Melamed, Vice President Government Affairs, The Washington Post, 1150 15th Street, N.W., Washington, D.C. 20071 by December 2, 1997.

-  You must agree to be bound by the decision of the arbitrator.

Please answer the questions on this Claim Form to the best of your ability. If you have any questions, please call the Guild (at 202-393-0808) or Carol Melamed (at 202-334-6105). If necessary, to complete your answers, use the other side of the form or additional pieces of paper. Consistent with the Post's policy against retaliation and the requirements of law, employees will not be subject to retaliation for filing a claim or participating in a proceeding.
